lead: A signal constellation is a drawing of every waveform a modulator can send, plotted as points in a two-dimensional signal space built from two orthonormal basis functions. That one picture answers two exam questions at once: how far apart the points are, which sets the error probability, and how many points there are, which sets bits per symbol and bandwidth efficiency. Every passband modem, from BPSK on a satellite link to 1024-QAM in Wi-Fi, is designed on this picture.
prereq: You need: signal-space vectors and the orthonormal basis from Unit 5, plus the BPSK, QPSK and QAM modulators of 6.2, 6.4 and 6.5.

blocks.text: A passband symbol lasts T_s seconds at carrier frequency f_c. Two orthonormal basis functions carry all of it: φ₁(t) = √(2/T_s)·cos(2πf_c t) and φ₂(t) = −√(2/T_s)·sin(2πf_c t), defined for 0 ≤ t < T_s. Each has unit energy, and their product integrates to zero over one symbol.

Any symbol waveform is s_i(t) = s_i1·φ₁(t) + s_i2·φ₂(t). The pair (s_i1, s_i2) plots as one point on the I–Q plane: I is the in-phase axis, Q the quadrature axis. Symbol energy is E_si = s_i1² + s_i2², the squared length of that vector. Averaged over M equally likely symbols, E_s = (1/M)·Σ E_si.

The receiver correlates the incoming signal with both basis functions and gets a noisy point r = (r₁, r₂). It decides for the nearest constellation point. All received points closer to s_i than to any other symbol form the decision region of s_i; these regions are the Voronoi cells of the constellation.

blocks.where: d_ij is the Euclidean distance between symbols i and j; s_i1, s_i2 are the I and Q components of symbol i (volts or √joule, depending on normalization).

blocks.text: The smallest of those distances is the minimum Euclidean distance, d_min = min over i≠j of d_ij. It is the one number that sets error probability: a symbol is misread when noise pushes the received point across the nearest decision boundary, which sits d_min/2 away.

blocks.where: N_nb is the number of nearest neighbours of a point; N₀/2 is the two-sided power spectral density of the AWGN; Q(x) = (1/√(2π))·∫ₓ^∞ e^(−u²/2) du is the Gaussian tail probability.

blocks.text: BPSK has two points at ±√E_b, so d_min = 2√E_b and P_b = Q(√(2E_b/N₀)), the exact result of 6.2. QPSK has four points at (±√(E_s/2), ±√(E_s/2)), so d_min = √(2E_s) = 2√E_b, because E_s = 2E_b. In terms of E_b it is the same distance as BPSK, hence the same P_b, but it carries two bits per symbol.
16-QAM takes I and Q from ±a, ±3a. Then E_s = 10a² and d_min = 2a, so d_min² = 0.4E_s = 1.6E_b. Against 4E_b for BPSK the ratio is 2.5, which is 4 dB. That is the price of four bits per symbol.

sections.h3: Size sets the bits and the bandwidth

blocks.text: Constellation size M sets the bits per symbol k = log₂ M, and the bit rate R_b = k·R_s, where R_s = 1/T_s is the symbol rate in symbols per second (baud). Bandwidth efficiency is η = R_b/B, where B is the occupied channel bandwidth in hertz. It is bits per second per hertz, never bits per symbol.

With rectangular pulses the baseband envelope is a sinc whose first null is at R_s; after modulation the passband main lobe is 2R_s wide, so B = 2R_s and η = k·R_s/(2R_s) = k/2. With ideal Nyquist shaping (sinc pulses, roll-off zero) the passband bandwidth is only R_s, giving η = k.
Plot η across and required E_b/N₀ up the side. That plane shows the trade directly: moving right means more bits per hertz, moving down means less power per bit.

QAM and PSK sit on the bandwidth-efficient side, reaching η = k/2 with rectangular pulses. The power bill is steep: at the same P_b, going from QPSK to 16-QAM to 64-QAM costs about 4 dB from QPSK to 16-QAM and about 4.5 dB from 16-QAM to 64-QAM, because d_min² drops from 4E_b to 1.6E_b to 0.57E_b. A 256-QAM Wi-Fi link therefore runs only when the phone is close to the router.

MFSK sits on the other side. Its M orthogonal tones need bandwidth that grows with M, so η falls as k rises, but its d_min grows with M, so the required E_b/N₀ falls. Deep-space and low-power telemetry links choose it.

The Shannon limit is the boundary of this plane: η ≤ log₂(1 + SNR), which rewritten per bit gives E_b/N₀ ≥ (2^η − 1)/η, with a floor of −1.59 dB as η → 0. It marks what is impossible, not how to build a modem.

figure.caption: BPSK uses two points on the I axis, QPSK the four corners, and 16-QAM a 4 by 4 grid. The 16-QAM grid reaches ±3 while the BPSK points sit at ±1; if all three were scaled to the same average energy, the 16-QAM points would be much closer together.

spec.aria: BPSK points lie on the I axis, QPSK points sit at four corners, and 16-QAM points fill a 4 by 4 grid.

examples.question: A 10 MHz passband channel carries rectangular-pulse modulation whose null-to-null bandwidth is B = 2R_s. Find the symbol rate, and the maximum bit rate and bandwidth efficiency for BPSK, QPSK and 16-QAM. State which scheme needs the largest E_b/N₀ for the same bit error probability.
steps: Given B = 10 MHz = 10 × 10⁶ Hz and B = 2R_s, so R_s = B/2 = 5 × 10⁶ sym/s = 5 Msym/s.
BPSK: k = log₂2 = 1 bit/symbol. R_b = k·R_s = 1 × 5 × 10⁶ = 5 Mbps. η = R_b/B = 5 × 10⁶ / (10 × 10⁶) = 0.5 bps/Hz, which equals k/2.
QPSK: k = log₂4 = 2 bits/symbol. R_b = 2 × 5 × 10⁶ = 10 Mbps. η = 10 × 10⁶ / (10 × 10⁶) = 1 bps/Hz.
16-QAM: k = log₂16 = 4 bits/symbol. R_b = 4 × 5 × 10⁶ = 20 Mbps. η = 20 × 10⁶ / (10 × 10⁶) = 2 bps/Hz.
Power check: d_min² = 4E_b for BPSK and QPSK, but 1.6E_b for 16-QAM. The ratio 4/1.6 = 2.5 is 10·log₁₀2.5 ≈ 4 dB, so 16-QAM needs about 4 dB more E_b/N₀ for the same P_b.
examples.answer: R_s = 5 Msym/s; BPSK gives 5 Mbps at η = 0.5 bps/Hz, QPSK 10 Mbps at η = 1 bps/Hz, and 16-QAM 20 Mbps at η = 2 bps/Hz, with 16-QAM needing about 4 dB more E_b/N₀ for the same error probability.
examples.check:
B = 10e6
Rs = B / 2
print(Rs / 1e6)
for k in (1, 2, 4):
    print(k * Rs / 1e6)
    print(k * Rs / B)

traps: Do not use the baseband Nyquist bandwidth R_s/2 for a passband channel. The passband minimum is R_s, so η = k with ideal shaping and only k/2 with a rectangular pulse.
η is bits per second per hertz, not bits per symbol. QPSK carries 2 bits per symbol but has η = 1 bps/Hz on a rectangular-pulse channel.

Compare schemes at the same E_b/N₀, not the same E_s/N₀. 16-QAM at the same E_s as QPSK has 3 dB less energy per bit, because E_s = 2E_b for QPSK but E_s = 4E_b for 16-QAM, so E_b halves; its P_b is far worse. The 6 dB figure applies only when 16-QAM is compared with BPSK at the same E_s.
d_min is a distance; d_min² is what most tables list. The Q-function argument uses d_min/√(2N₀), not d_min².
QPSK is not noisier than BPSK. At equal E_b/N₀ the two have the same P_b; QPSK simply carries twice the bits in the same bandwidth.

quiz.q: Define d_min and average symbol energy E_s for an M-point constellation.
quiz.a: d_min = min over i≠j of √((s_i1 − s_j1)² + (s_i2 − s_j2)²), the smallest distance between any two points. E_s = (1/M)·Σ(s_i1² + s_i2²), the mean squared vector length.

quiz.q: How many bits per symbol does 16-QAM carry, and what is its bandwidth efficiency when B = 2R_s?
quiz.a: k = log₂16 = 4 bits per symbol; η = k/2 = 2 bps/Hz.

quiz.q: Why does raising M at fixed E_s reduce the noise margin?
quiz.a: More points must share the same average energy, so the nearest-neighbour spacing d_min shrinks. The Q-function argument d_min/√(2N₀) falls, and P_e rises.

quiz.q: A 200 kHz passband channel uses 64-QAM with rectangular pulses and B = 2R_s. Find R_s, R_b and η.
16-QAM has d_min² = 1.6E_b and BPSK has d_min² = 4E_b. How much extra E_b/N₀ does 16-QAM need for the same P_b?
quiz.a: Ratio = 4/1.6 = 2.5, so the extra power is 10·log₁₀2.5 ≈ 4 dB.

quiz.q: BPSK and QPSK both have d_min² = 4E_b, yet QPSK doubles η. Explain where the extra bits come from.
quiz.a: QPSK uses a second orthonormal basis function, so its two bits travel on two independent I and Q dimensions of the same symbol interval. Each dimension carries one antipodal bit with the same d_min, so the error probability is unchanged while two bits occupy one symbol slot.

quiz.q: Why does MFSK have poor bandwidth efficiency but good power efficiency, while QAM is the reverse?
quiz.a: MFSK uses M orthogonal tones, so its bandwidth grows roughly in proportion to M while the bit rate grows only as log₂M; η falls. Its points are far apart in M-dimensional space, so d_min grows and required E_b/N₀ falls. QAM packs points densely in two dimensions: high η, small d_min, high power demand.

beyond: Not for the exam. Real standards choose the constellation from a table while the link runs: Wi-Fi and 4G step between QPSK and 256-QAM or 1024-QAM as the measured SNR rises, which is adaptive modulation and coding. The remaining gap to the Shannon limit is closed by coding (Unit 7) and, more recently, by constellation shaping: geometric shaping moves the point positions, probabilistic shaping changes how often each point is used. Search for "adaptive modulation and coding", "probabilistic amplitude shaping" and "geometric constellation shaping".
